learningObjective: Diagnose external fragmentation in a contiguous per-sequence KV allocator vs paged allocation.

canonicalClaims.claim: Contiguous per-sequence KV slabs sized to max_new_tokens cause both internal waste (reserved but not-yet-used positions) and external fragmentation (freed slabs of varying sizes leave non-contiguous holes). PagedAttention eliminates external fragmentation via fixed-size block + block-table indirection.
conditions: Per-sequence slabs allocated up-front at max_new_tokens size.
Sequences have varying max_new_tokens and lifetimes.
nonImplications: Does not imply paged KV has zero waste (small internal waste per sequence remains).
Does not imply paging solves scheduling problems by itself.

misconceptions.claim: OOM with free memory reported is always an accounting bug.
misconceptions.whyWrong: External fragmentation legitimately produces this pattern.

misconceptions.claim: KV OOM is a data-race between scheduler and allocator.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Fragmentation is deterministic given allocation policy.

misconceptions.claim: TP helps KV OOM by making decode faster.
misconceptions.whyWrong: TP shards weights and slightly shrinks per-GPU KV footprint by factor T, but does not address fragmentation.

implementationFacts: vLLM's PagedAttention allocates 16-token blocks; residual internal waste is bounded by 15 tokens per sequence.
External fragmentation was measured as ~60-80% memory waste in prior systems in the vLLM paper.
performanceScenarios: Heterogeneous max_new_tokens is the worst case for contiguous allocation.
Paged allocation is essentially the OS virtual-memory analog applied to KV cache.
